Reuters US Domestic News Summary Reuters | Updated: 04-10-2026 18:28 IST | Created: 04-10-2026 18:28 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Following is a summary of current US domestic news briefs. Judge bars building of Texas-Mexico border barrier in Big Bend National Park A federal judge on Friday barred the Trump administration from building a US-Mexico border barrier through Big Bend National Park in Texas while courts consider an environmental lawsuit challenging the project. The ruling came nearly seven weeks after US Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott paused construction amid bipartisan criticism of the border project and its potential impact on the park's landscape and wildlife. Japan's Takaichi protests to US after Marine accused of murder in Okinawa Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered a protest with the United States on Sunday after a US Marine was arrested on suspicion of robbing and murdering a Japanese woman in Okinawa. Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southernmost prefecture, on Saturday and taking her wallet and backpack, police said. Ballard denied the allegations, police said. Trump picks John Coale as special presidential envoy for hostage affairs US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that lawyer and current Belarus envoy John Coale, who has been credited with the release of hundreds of prisoners, would be his special presidential envoy for hostage affairs. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko pardoned 15 prisoners last month after talks with Coale, who has been talking to Minsk for more than a year. Exclusive-ShinyHunters hacker in FBI data theft detained in Jordan, cooperating with bureau, sources say A suspected member of the ShinyHunters hacking group, which says it stole data on every FBI employee, was detained in Jordan this week and is cooperating with the FBI, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters. Saif al-Din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities, the three sources said. Two of them said he was brought into custody on Tuesday. Reuters could not immediately determine the circumstances of Khader’s detention or where he is being held. Two sources said that he is helping the FBI and global law enforcement locate the other hackers in the group. Exclusive-Trump visa policies weigh on Columbia journalism program as admissions pause The Trump administration's changing visa policies caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its journalism programs, four people familiar with the matter said. The journalism school announced on Thursday it was pausing admissions to its Master of Arts offering to conduct a "critical evaluation," without giving further details about the reasons. New term gives US Supreme Court's Thomas and Alito more chances to wield power The new US Supreme Court term that begins on Monday presents opportunities for its two eldest and most conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, to help push US law further rightward on contentious issues such as gun rights, religion in public schools and voting restrictions. Thomas, 78, has served on the top US judicial body since 1991, making him the second-longest-serving justice in American history. Alito, 76, has served since 2006. In crude Ohio rally speech, Trump says he may not help if Democrats win US President Donald Trump used an Ohio rally on Saturday to mix profane attacks on Democrats with promises of financial help if Republicans win the midterms and a warning that he would be less willing to work with the state if Democrats prevail. "Just get out and vote," Trump said at a rally for Republican candidates, including US Senator Jon Husted and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. "If you do that, we're going to win, and we're going to win big, and we're going to shove it up their ass." Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid demolition fight This year's Kennedy Center Honors will be held at Washington's Capital One Arena as the Trump administration faces legal and congressional challenges over plans to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, a center spokesperson said on Friday. This will be the first time the honors are not held at the center's Opera House since the awards' inception in 1978. Former US congressman sentenced to 10 years for secretly lobbying for Venezuela Former US Congressman David Rivera was sentenced to 10 years in prison on Friday for illegally lobbying US officials to ease pressure on ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro's government. Rivera, a Republican who represented southern Florida in the US House of Representatives from 2011 to 2013, was convicted at trial in May of lobbying US officials on Venezuela's behalf in 2017 without registering as a foreign lobbyist as required by the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA). With a mixed scorecard, Trump poised to test his powers again at US Supreme Court The US Supreme Court begins its new nine-month term on Monday much as it ended its last one, confronted with more cases involving President Donald Trump's far-reaching policies and aggressive uses of power that will keep testing how far the justices will let him expand his authority. The court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, wrapped up its last term in June, one dominated by legal battles centered on Trump's exertion of presidential powers. The justices gave the Republican president several major wins and a few big losses. Cornell president vows 'serious look' at fraternities, sororities in wake of rape allegations Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus following an outcry over the school's handling of a student's rape allegations, the Ivy League school's president said on Saturday. A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman, who alleges she was drugged and raped in 2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has sparked outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the school in Ithaca, New York. Tennessee prison chief resigns after failed execution The head of the Tennessee Department of Correction will step down this month, state officials said on Saturday, days after convicted murderer Christa Pike was left gravely ill from the state's failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection. The botched execution on Wednesday left Pike unconscious, intubated and hooked to a mechanical ventilator to breathe, her lawyers wrote in a Friday court filing. It is the state's second failed execution attempt this year, prompting Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to halt attempts to carry out the death penalty for the rest of 2026. NY governor attacks law enforcement's handling of 2024 Cornell rape investigation New York Governor Kathy Hochul on Friday faulted police and prosecutors for failing to fully investigate an alleged gang rape in 2024 at Cornell University, saying she was "deeply disturbed" by how the incident was handled. Hochul was speaking at a press conference alongside state Attorney General Letitia James, whom she appointed on Thursday night as a special prosecutor to investigate the allegations. Fed may skip October but pull rate hike trigger in December Federal Reserve policymakers were already leaning against delivering a second straight rate hike this month to give them time to sift through more economic data before pulling the trigger again, and a cooler than expected job market report Friday leaves that approach intact. Still-to-come data, particularly the closely-watched consumer price index measure of inflation coming just before the Fed's October 27-28 policy meeting, could yet shift that calculus. At Cornell, rape allegations spark outrage, soul-searching over campus culture Cornell University student Sophia Riley Sim skipped classes this week, consumed by allegations in a lawsuit that several members of a fraternity raped a young woman in 2024 and troubled by how her university handled the case. "Cornell has failed our community through its lack of accountability, transparency, and failure to address the state of the Cornell student body at this time," Sim, a junior, said at a public hearing on sexual assault organized by Cornell's Student Assembly on Thursday. Tennessee execution survivor Christa Pike unconscious on ventilator, lawyers say Convicted killer Christa Pike was left gravely ill, unconscious and hospitalized on life support after Tennessee's failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said on Friday, providing the first detailed account of the injuries she suffered. Hospital staff were working to save Pike's life and clear the drug pentobarbital from her system, her attorneys said in an emergency motion, which seeks a court order for Tennessee's Department of Correction to preserve evidence from Wednesday night's botched execution. Aboard the USS George Washington, young sailors adjust to war with Iran An emergency alert blares from a loudspeaker, and Damon Dennard and other sailors on the deck of the aircraft carrier USS George Washington are scrambling. Dennard, 23, is readying bombs for loading onto aircraft as his crewmates race to their positions. "It has been eventful," says Dennard, an aviation ordnanceman airman apprentice. Once the alert ends, he takes a breath, sits on one of the bombs and jokes that he probably expected an easier deployment. Bipartisan members of Congress move to block demolition of Kennedy Center When President Donald Trump took a wrecking ball to the East Wing of the White House, it took Washington by surprise. Now, there is a move in the US Congress to avoid a second such surprise with legislation to prohibit him from demolishing the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The maneuver comes on the heels of a federal judge ordering the Trump administration to provide at least 30 days' notice before taking steps to demolish the building. Trump himself had told reporters in mid-September that unless his name was on the Kennedy Center, "It's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down." Pennsylvania measles cases near 1,000 as outbreak spreads Pennsylvania's health department reported 977 measles cases as of Friday, according to its website, as the state continues to battle a fast-growing outbreak of the disease. Here are more details: US Supreme Court to kick off term with bid by Big Oil to toss climate suits The US Supreme Court begins its new nine-month term on Monday with arguments in a major case involving a bid by oil companies ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy to scuttle a lawsuit by officials in Boulder, Colorado, seeking monetary damages for harms caused by climate change. It is the first of several important cases already teed up for the term, with disputes involving issues such as President Donald Trump's immigration policies and state-level bans on assault-style rifles to be heard in the coming months. The court's 6-3 conservative majority has moved US law dramatically rightward in recent years. US Coast Guard finds debris from missing medical aircraft off Nantucket The US Coast Guard said late on Saturday it found debris from a medical transport aircraft off the shore of Massachusetts' Nantucket island and was searching for six people who were on board. The Federal Aviation Administration told the Coast Guard early on Saturday that it had lost contact with a Gulfstream jet traveling from Bermuda to Boston. Several hours later, the Coast Guard said in a statement that it "located a debris field that has been confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft."

item.title: “I don’t go to sets with a phone": Paul Rudd reveals his new habit during movie shoots
item.description: Actor Paul Rudd revealed that he doesn't take his phone on the sets of the film because he is addicted to it, Variety reported.
item.content:encoded:
“I don’t go to sets with a phone": Paul Rudd reveals his new habit during movie shoots  Actor Paul Rudd revealed that he doesn't take his phone on the sets of the film because he is addicted to it, Variety reported.  ANI | Updated: 04-10-2026 17:23 IST | Created: 04-10-2026 17:23 IST

Paul Rudd (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Actor Paul Rudd revealed that he doesn't take his phone on the sets of the film because he is addicted to it, Variety reported. The actor is set to play the moderator of the first-ever meeting dedicated to solving America’s climate crisis in “A Statement,” the latest film from Oscar-winning director Tom McCarthy. Set at a Florida beachside resort in 1980, the film follows 20 experts who spend a weekend in a conference room and figure out their differences over how to draft a statement to Congress about the effects of carbon dioxide emissions on the climate, reported Variety. The cast includes Paul Giamatti, Tatiana Maslany and John Turturro and the actor admitted that he feels more connected to the ensemble cast by leaving his smartphone in his trailer, a practice he claims he’s now followed for some time. “I don’t go to sets with a phone. I haven’t done that for a while now. It’s important to put it down. Anytime. They’re horrible things. I’m addicted to it like everybody else. They’re facilitating our own destruction,” he told Variety Saturday evening during the film’s world premiere at the New York Film Festival. Rudd revealed that director McCarthy enforced a “very strict no phones policy” on the set of “A Statement,” which he found brought his castmates closer together and made filming feel more like a play. “The world has changed since cell phones have existed. We don’t look at each other or talk to each other quite the same way. Now, [with the phone ban], we were forced to really spend time with each other and talk. Working on a movie set in 1980, we’re dressed in a certain kind of way. It felt like, ‘Oh, yeah. I remember this. This feels like it used to feel when people sat around and spoke to one another,’” added Paul Rudd, as quoted by Variety. (ANI)

item.description: By Ben Makori SHERFIELD ON LODDON, England, Oct 4 (Reuters) - F lydubai's flight FZ1073, which plunged 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, would have felt ...
item.content:encoded:
Like a 'vertical roller coaster': Simulating flight FZ1073's sudden plunge Reuters | Updated: 04-10-2026 15:26 IST | Created: 04-10-2026 15:26 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

By Ben Makori SHERFIELD ON LODDON, England, Oct 4 (Reuters) - F lydubai's flight FZ1073, which plunged 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, would have felt like a "vertical roller coaster", according to an aviation instructor who recreated the descent in a flight simulator for Reuters. The steep fall, after an attack on the captain by the co-pilot during a flight on Wednesday, would have put huge strain on the Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft - as well as the passengers and crew, said Alberto Paduanelli, owner of ALPA Simulation in Sherfield on Loddon, southern England. The co-pilot of the flydubai jet, which was bound for Israel from Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, calling the incident a "terrorist attack". The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, two sources with knowledge of the investigation told Reuters. UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity. Reuters could not independently reach al-Hammami for comment. Flydubai says the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation and it cannot comment further. Oman has yet to comment on the incident. "A plunge of 16,000 feet (4,877 metres) over 30 seconds will feel like you are over on a very, very vertical roller coaster," Paduanelli said, sitting at the controls of the simulator cockpit. "The difference is that on the roller coaster, you know what's happening," he said, adding that with a sudden drop "you feel the negative g-force on your body". For passengers who are not strapped in, "Your body will literally lift from the seat", he said. Using a simulator to recreate the incident, Paduanelli said the aircraft's autopilot disconnected before the plunge began, causing the jet to accelerate rapidly. US President Donald Trump has praised the Boeing jet for withstanding the severe forces put on it during the incident. The plane was levelled out after passengers overpowered the co-pilot, before a reserve crew of pilots onboard landed the plane. "It was an amazing show of precise and powerful structural planning and design," Trump posted on Truth Social, adding that the 737 Max "was able to withstand G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to do". Boeing did not respond to a request for comment. Aircraft are designed and tested to withstand substantial aerodynamic loads, but Paduanelli said a prolonged high-speed dive can place extreme strain on an airframe. "This was nothing but a miracle that nothing was hurt apart from the captain, unfortunately, and that two pilots were onboard," Paduanelli said. Details about al-Hammami's past have trickled out. Royal Air Maroc told Reuters he did a three-month training with the airline in 2025 but his application to work there afterwards was rejected. Buckinghamshire New University in Britain said he did a distance-learning course in aviation management with the institution, but no pilot training. An Australian Federal Police spokesperson said on Sunday that authorities there were investigating al-Hammami's "links to Australia". A source briefed on the investigation said the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne.

item.title: US Senator warns China’s pressure on Taiwan could threaten global travel
item.description: US Senator Tammy Duckworth warned that China pressured Madagascar, Mauritius, and Seychelles to deny airspace clearance to Taiwan's presidential aircraft, setting a dangerous global precedent. While ...
item.content:encoded:
US Senator warns China’s pressure on Taiwan could threaten global travel US Senator Tammy Duckworth warned that China pressured Madagascar, Mauritius, and Seychelles to deny airspace clearance to Taiwan's presidential aircraft, setting a dangerous global precedent. While nominee Marc Dillard called the impact limited, Duckworth stressed that it threatens international aviation, trade, and sovereignty. ANI | Updated: 04-10-2026 14:31 IST | Created: 04-10-2026 14:31 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US Senator Tammy Duckworth has warned that China’s efforts to pressure countries into restricting Taiwan’s international travel could set a dangerous precedent for global aviation, trade and international movement. According to a report published by Taipei Times, Duckworth raised the issue during a US Senate Foreign Relations Committee nominations hearing, where she questioned Marc Dillard, the nominee for US ambassador to Madagascar and Comoros, over Beijing’s efforts to isolate Taiwan. Duckworth said Madagascar, Mauritius and Seychelles had in April withdrawn permission for Taiwanese President William Lai’s aircraft to use airspace under their control. The move delayed Lai’s journey to Taiwan’s diplomatic ally Eswatini and, according to the senator, was carried out at China’s behest. The Taipei Times reported that Madagascar and Mauritius later interfered with arrangements for Lai’s return journey as well. Duckworth argued that such restrictions were inconsistent with international aviation rules and said Taiwanese officials had repeatedly raised the matter during her recent visit to Taiwan. “These reckless actions could endanger everyone who travels internationally,” Duckworth said, warning that China’s pressure could eventually extend beyond Taiwanese presidential aircraft to planes carrying civilians or critical supplies. Dillard, who is currently deputy chief of mission at the US Embassy in South Africa, acknowledged that the episode reflected what he described as Beijing’s broader intimidation tactics. However, he characterised the immediate impact on Lai’s flight as limited. As reported by Taipei Times, Dillard said that Madagascar’s withdrawal of clearance undermined the country’s ability to make sovereign foreign-policy decisions. He added that, if confirmed as ambassador, he would engage Madagascar’s government on the risks associated with deepening ties with China and highlight the benefits of maintaining the US as a trusted partner. Duckworth challenged the description of the disruption as “limited”, noting that Lai had been forced to alter his flight path. The Taipei Times report quoted Duckworth as warning that the issue went beyond a single presidential journey. She said the international community must ensure countries continue to respect established aviation arrangements, cautioning that similar pressure could eventually affect territorial waters and international trade. In a statement issued Thursday, Duckworth’s office said the episode demonstrated the urgent need for continued US support for Taiwan in the face of Chinese pressure. (ANI)
